title: Comments and constants: give a number a meaning
goal: Distinguish a literal, a name and an object; express a unit rule and write a comment that explains why.

prerequisites.text: The first-program scaffold, named int quantities, output, and naming rules from the previous lessons.
Multiplication and subtraction of small integers. Types are treated next; you do not need to write functions, macros, or templates.

sections.title: Two numbers with different jobs
paragraphs: A lesson lasts 25 minutes, but the report needs seconds. The formula contains 25 and 60. If the timetable changes, which number describes the lesson and which describes the units?
Give the two numbers different names before calculating. In the example, identify the value that changes with the timetable and the conversion factor that stays the same.

reveal.title: Compare your prediction and follow the steps
paragraphs: In const int lessonMinutes = 25;, 25 is a literal and lessonMinutes is a name; the declaration creates an int object with that initial value. A type determines values and operations. int suffices for the small whole numbers here; a fuller type treatment follows next.

Two occurrences of 60 may mean seconds per minute and an age limit. Combining them under one name merely because the numbers match is wrong. Choose a name for the domain meaning. secondsPerMinute expresses a minutes-to-seconds factor; generalValue does not.

Change only the explanatory comment: stdout should stay the same. In a separate experiment, change the duration to 30 minutes: expect duration_s=1800. These are two experiments, not one question with two answers.

tables.caption: Follow the difficult step
rows: A different initial value may be chosen
A new run can create it with a new duration

sections.title: What const prevents
paragraphs: const int lessonMinutes = 25; initializes a simple integer object whose value cannot later be replaced by ordinary assignment such as lessonMinutes = 30;. Initialization supplies the first value; assignment tries to replace an existing one. The negative example below deliberately tests a build error.

const alone does not require the initial value to be known at compile time: it may be obtained during execution. A fixed number in our example does not turn const into a universal instruction to precompute. We do not introduce runtime input merely to demonstrate this; its rules belong in the standard-I/O lesson.

sections.title: When constexpr is appropriate
paragraphs: constexpr int secondsPerHour = 60 * 60; requires a valid constant expression as its initializer. The operands are known, the multiplication is permitted, and 3600 fits in int. The object is also const, so later assignment is prohibited. This makes the intention explicit for fixed conversion factors.

This is a rule about allowed expressions, not an optimizer stopwatch. Do not claim that const is always slower than constexpr or that every occurrence forces a separate build-time operation. We are not writing constexpr functions, #define macros, or metaprograms here.

sections.title: Different spellings of the same value
paragraphs: 1024 and 1'024 denote the same value: an apostrophe within the number separates digits and is not printed. A separator cannot be placed arbitrarily before the first or after the last digit. 1,024 is not the same literal; a comma has other C++ roles. Decimal fractions in source use a dot, as in 2.5.

The 0b prefix introduces binary notation: 0b1010 = 8 + 2 = 10. Ordinary std::cout output of int remains decimal and prints 10. Hexadecimal uses 0x, but this lesson is not a full number-base course. Avoid 010 when you mean ten: a leading zero introduces octal notation. Prefer decimal notation for ordinary quantities.

sections.title: Characters, strings and control characters
paragraphs: In const char grade = 'A';, char is a character type for one code unit, and single quotes introduce an ordinary character literal. "A" in double quotes is a string literal, with a different type and representation. A word does not fit in one char. Ordinary char is not a container for every Unicode character: a Russian letter encoded in UTF-8 can occupy multiple bytes.

\n denotes newline, \t a tab, \\ one backslash, and \" a quote within a string. The path example escapes the backslash in C:\temp; otherwise \t would become a tab. Quotes and backslashes in source are notation rather than an instruction to print every source character. Predict actual stdout instead of copying the source literal.

sections.title: A comment answers “why”
paragraphs: // begins a comment through the end of the line. /* and */ delimit a block comment; block comments do not nest. Inside a string literal, "//" is ordinary text. A comment is not executed, but removing it carelessly can join separate tokens. Keep the intended token boundary.

“Multiply by 60” repeats a visible operation. “The schedule records whole minutes; the report requires seconds” explains a unit contract. A comment about equipment explains why two seats are reserved. When policy changes, review both the comment and value. An obsolete explanation can make a wrong formula seem justified.

sections.title: Changing the spelling while preserving the meaning
paragraphs: Record the original result. Determine the factor’s meaning, declare a name, replace corresponding uses, and compare output. Not every zero or newline needs a separate name. Naming helps when it explains a domain rule or prevents inconsistent changes.

Names do not validate units automatically. After the minutes-to-seconds review, test 0, 15, and 40 minutes again. The diagram connects the domain concept, value notation, and use. It does not prove when a compiler evaluated an expression.

sections.title: Intentional: changing a constant
paragraphs: This is a separate faulty program for examining a diagnostic. It does not replace your work. Locate the cause first, then compare the build failure with a corrected version.
An existing const int cannot be changed by this assignment.

sections.title: Intentional: a string in place of char
paragraphs: This is a separate faulty program for examining a diagnostic. It does not replace your work. Locate the cause first, then compare the build failure with a corrected version.
Double quotes produce a string literal. This example needs single quotes for one ordinary character.

deep.title: Can const get its value while the program runs?
deep.text: Yes. In the input lesson you will be able to read a value and then use it to initialise a const object. The restriction on modifying that object applies after construction regardless of when the number became known. constexpr adds a requirement on the initial expression.

sections.title: Now solve a different problem
paragraphs: Refactor the conversion of 15 minutes to seconds. Preserve stdout, introduce secondsPerMinute and lessonMinutes, and add a comment explaining the unit contract. Also represent room A as a char and separately as a string followed by a newline. Explain the quotation marks. In a separate copy, check 1'024 and 0b1010 without changing the main task’s minutes-to-seconds contract.
Open Practice. Its starter and your current source are separate from the worked examples. Write a prediction before running, then explain the result in your own words.

selfcheck.prompt: Only the comment text changes in the 25 minutes × 60 example; declarations and output stay unchanged. What is stdout?
feedback: Correct: this comment edit does not change the calculation.
1800 follows a change to 30 minutes; this experiment edits only the comment.
The program prints the labelled product, not the two operands.

execution.label: predict

selfcheck.prompt: What does const enforce for our simple integer objects?
options: Every initial value is evaluated during the build
Ordinary assignment cannot change the object after initialization
selfcheck.feedback: const restricts mutation; it does not generally require a constant-expression initializer.

selfcheck.prompt: What does int n = 0b1010; std::cout << n; print without format changes?
selfcheck.feedback: 0b sets source notation; ordinary integer output here is decimal.

selfcheck.prompt: Why do const int cmPerMeter = 100; and const int attendeeLimit = 100; have different names?
options: One is a unit rule and the other an independent policy
selfcheck.feedback: Meaning determines the role: the limit can change independently of the metric system.

selfcheck.prompt: What does \n mean in the source string "A\n"?
options: Two printed characters: backslash and n
selfcheck.feedback: The escape denotes a control character inside the literal and is unrelated to return 0.

selfcheck.prompt: Also represent room A as a char and separately as a string followed by a newline. Explain the quotation marks. In a separate copy, check 1'024 and 0b1010 without changing the main task’s minutes-to-seconds contract.
selfcheck.feedback: Explain in words which object or intermediate value changes. Matching stdout does not replace that explanation.

practice.title: A unit contract without magic numbers
practice.task: Refactor the conversion of 15 minutes to seconds. Preserve stdout, introduce secondsPerMinute and lessonMinutes, and add a comment explaining the unit contract. Also represent room A as a char and separately as a string followed by a newline. Explain the quotation marks. In a separate copy, check 1'024 and 0b1010 without changing the main task’s minutes-to-seconds contract.
criteria: Both names express roles and the factor is specified once.
Explain const versus constexpr without a speed claim.
Record actual outputs of 0, 900, and 2400 seconds.
The comment matches the formula; the const diagnostic is separate from the working solution.
Explain in words which object or intermediate value changes. Matching stdout does not replace that explanation.
practice.hint: Also represent room A as a char and separately as a string followed by a newline. Explain the quotation marks. In a separate copy, check 1'024 and 0b1010 without changing the main task’s minutes-to-seconds contract.

steps.action: Separate the fixed factor from this scenario’s parameter.
Explain why units are converted, not what * does.
Test 0, 15, and 40 minutes with the same formula.
In a separate copy, trigger and repair an assignment-to-const error.

terms.definition: A value written directly in source: 60, 0b1010, 'A', or "done".
For the simple objects in this lesson, prevents changing the value after initialization by ordinary assignment.
In our integer constant declaration, requires a valid constant-expression initializer and makes the object const.
A source explanation rather than an executable statement; it must stay accurate when code changes.
A literal whose purpose or unit is unclear where it is used. Not every literal is automatically bad.
A notation for a special character within a literal, such as \n for newline or \\ for a backslash.
